method: Mains-powered tungsten, fluorescent and HMI lamps follow the supply voltage, so their light output ripples at twice the mains frequency: 100 Hz on a 50 Hz supply and 120 Hz on a 60 Hz supply, one pulse every 1 / ripple seconds. A camera frame integrates the light while the shutter is open, so an exposure that spans a whole number of pulses collects the same light in every frame, while the fractional remainder leaves a frame-to-frame brightness swing of roughly that fraction of the lamp's modulation. The page computes the exposure as shutter angle / (360 x frame rate), divides it by the ripple period to get the pulses covered, and calls the setting flicker-safe when the result is within 0.5% of a whole pulse; the leftover fraction is also reported as a percentage brightness swing. The whole-pulse shutter speeds are k / ripple for integer k, which at frame rate p correspond to the angles 360 x k x p / ripple; the page lists up to twelve of them that fit inside one frame and recommends the one whose exposure is closest to the entered target in stops, breaking a tie towards the shorter exposure. When the ripple is faster than a frame, no shutter angle can cover a whole pulse and the page names frame rates that divide the ripple instead. A custom ripple frequency covers dimmed LED fixtures whose driver rate differs from the mains ripple. Frame rates are limited to 1-240 fps, shutter angles to 1-360 degrees and custom frequencies to 10-2000 Hz. Rolling-shutter readout skew, aperture, ND filtration and camera-specific flicker filters are outside the model, and the result is a planning aid rather than a guarantee for a particular camera and lamp. Everything is computed in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

sources.title: Mains-powered tungsten, fluorescent and HMI lamps follow the supply voltage and ripple at twice the mains frequency, 100 Hz on a 50 Hz supply and 120 Hz on a 60 Hz supply.

A frame integrates light over its exposure, so an exposure spanning a whole number of ripple periods collects the same light every frame, and the fractional remainder sets the brightness swing between frames.
Exposure time is shutter angle / (360 x frames per second), the relation used in camera manuals such as the American Cinematographer Manual, ARRI and RED documentation.
The conventional workarounds are 172.8 degrees at 24 fps on a 50 Hz supply (1/50 s) and 144 degrees at 24 fps on a 60 Hz supply (1/60 s).
